opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to frame it right now is augmentation rather than replacement. A lot of the conversation jumps straight to "is this going to take my job," but what I see in practice is closer to an Iron Man suit than an Iron Man robot. The tools are very good at certain chunks of your work and surprisingly bad at others. It's a very jagged kind of intelligence. It can do something that looks superhuman one minute and then make a mistake no human would make the next.

So I'd encourage people to decompose their job into tasks. Some of those tasks are a great fit for the models today: drafting, summarizing, boilerplate code, searching through a lot of material, getting a first pass on something. Other tasks need judgment, taste, context about your organization, accountability, or a long chain of steps that has to be correct end to end. That second category is still very much the human's job.

I like to think about it as an autonomy slider. You can hand the model a little bit, like autocomplete, or a lot, like "go do this whole thing." Right now the sweet spot for most real work is somewhere in the middle. The AI generates, you verify, and you want that loop to be as fast as possible. A lot of the leverage comes from getting good at that loop: knowing how to prompt, how to give context, and how to quickly audit what comes back so you're not just accepting slop.

My practical advice is to just use these tools a lot. Get a feel for where they're strong and where they fall over, because that boundary moves every few months. The people who build that intuition early will be dramatically more productive. Over a longer horizon, sure, the slider moves toward more autonomy, and some jobs will change substantially. But I think it'll be more gradual than the hype suggests, because the last few nines of reliability are really hard. It's a bit like self-driving: a demo is easy, but a product that works all the time takes a long time. So I'd expect a decade-ish of humans and AIs working together, with the human role shifting toward supervising, directing, and verifying.

r001.rationale: The response says to decompose a job into tasks, identifies tasks AI handles well, and explains that using AI on those tasks makes people more productive.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most useful mental model is that AI tools are not replacing jobs, they're replacing tasks, and the fraction of your job that is exposed depends enormously on what the job actually is. Software engineering is probably the furthest along, because the data is abundant, the domain is text-based, and verification is cheap: you can run the code. That's why coding assistants got good first. Something like radiology, which everyone predicted would be automated a decade ago, turned out to be much messier, because the job is not just reading images, it's a whole tangle of liability, communication, and context that the models don't have access to.

So the first question I'd ask is: how much of what I do is verifiable, repeatable, and already written down somewhere? The more that's true, the faster the tools will eat into it. The second question is: what's my ratio of generation to judgment? These models are very good at generation and still quite unreliable at judgment. They'll produce a plausible-looking answer very quickly, and it's your job to know whether it's right. I actually think this is where a lot of people are getting burned right now. They over-trust the output, and the model is confidently wrong in ways that are hard to catch unless you already understand the domain.

Which leads to my practical advice, which is to use these things as a very capable intern that you supervise closely, rather than as an oracle. The people getting the most out of them are not the ones who hand over the whole task. They're the ones who break the task into chunks, keep the model on a short leash, verify constantly, and build up an intuition for where it's strong and where it falls apart. That intuition is genuinely a new skill, and I don't think it's a trivial one. It's a bit like learning to work with a very fast, very well-read collaborator who has no common sense and occasionally hallucinates.

The last thing I'd say is to resist both of the extreme narratives. The "nothing is happening, it's just autocomplete" view is wrong. I'm a decent programmer and my workflow has changed a lot in a couple of years. But the "everyone is unemployed in eighteen months" view is also wrong, because it ignores how much of the economy is tied up in slow, physical, high-trust, or regulated activity, and how long it takes to actually integrate a tool into real workflows. It's going to feel less like a cliff and more like a gradient that's steeper in some places than others, and your job is mostly to figure out where you're standing on it.

r001.rationale: The response frames AI’s impact as replacing or exposing particular tasks within a job, and says models generate answers quickly. It does not clearly explain the impact as accelerating some tasks within the job’s task bundle.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful way to think about it is to break your job down into tasks, because a job is usually a bundle of very different things. Some of those things are going to be very amenable to AI, and some of them still require a lot of context, judgment, or interaction with other people.

So I would encourage people to get hands-on. Take something you actually do during the day and try to do it with an AI tool. Where does it help? Where do you have to correct it? Where does checking its work take longer than doing it yourself? You want to develop an intuition for that boundary, because the capabilities are quite uneven.

Programming is a good example. You can delegate a piece of code, but you still have to know what you wanted, whether the result is correct, and how it fits into the larger system. Generating something and taking responsibility for it are different parts of the work.

And that boundary is moving. So I wouldn’t treat one disappointing interaction as a permanent verdict. The practical thing today is to learn how to delegate to these tools while retaining enough understanding to supervise them. That’s becoming a skill in its own right.

r001.rationale: The response frames jobs as bundles of tasks and says some are amenable to AI, but it does not clearly say AI accelerates some of those tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to think about it is at the level of tasks, rather than entire jobs. Your job is this bundle of things you do, and AI is going to be very good at some of those things, somewhat useful at others, and completely unreliable at others. So the question is: can you break down your work and figure out where this tool actually helps?

With programming, for example, I can delegate a lot of the typing, but I still have to decide what I want, give it enough context, and check that the result makes sense. Sometimes checking is easy, and you get a huge speedup. Sometimes checking is harder than doing the work yourself. That distinction matters a lot.

So I would encourage people to get hands-on with these tools in their actual work. You need to develop an intuition for their capabilities and their failure modes. And I think that intuition—knowing what to delegate, what to verify, and when to take over—is increasingly going to be part of being good at your job.

r001.rationale: The response describes a job as a bundle of tasks and says AI can be very useful for some tasks, with programming delegation sometimes producing a huge speedup.
